cards.explanation: The answer is that they are dull of hearing. The writer says it is hard to explain “…because you are dull of hearing.” He doesn't blame the roads or the schedule. He names the problem right to their faces, friends, and I think that took some nerve.

The answer is teachers. The writer says that by this time they ought to be teachers, but instead they need someone to reteach them the basic principles of God's word. That's like a cookie shop where the head baker still needs the oven explained to him. I would know, friends, I've had my share of oven confusion.

The answer is False. The writer says plainly, “You need milk, not solid food!” He says it right after telling them they need someone to reteach them the basics. He's not insulting the milk, friends. He's telling them where they are.

The answer is an infant. The writer says everyone who lives on milk is still an infant, inexperienced in the message of righteousness. Milk is where an infant starts, and the writer says solid food is for the mature. It's a picture of someone who still has growing to do.

The answer is good from evil. The writer says the mature “…by constant use have trained their senses to distinguish good from evil.” It's practice that does it, friends, not a one-time lesson. Like me and my stamping: the first batch came out a mess, and now I press clean without thinking.

The answer is True. The writer lists “…repentance from dead works, and of faith in God…” as part of the foundation (Hebrews 6:1). Faith in God sits right there in that first layer. Foundations aren't flashy, bakers, but nothing stands without one.

The answer is if God permits. The writer says, “And this we will do, if God permits.” I think he's saying the going on depends on God, not on how fired up they feel. A good baker still checks with the One who owns the kitchen.

The answer is that they crucify the Son of God all over again. The writer says these people are “…crucifying the Son of God all over again and subjecting Him to open shame.” Those are heavy words, friends, and I think they ought to feel heavy. This is a hard part of the passage.

The answer is True. The writer says land that drinks in the rain often falling on it and produces a crop useful to those for whom it is tended “…receives the blessing of God.” It's a simple picture, friends. Rain comes down, a useful crop comes up, and the blessing is there.

The answer is that it will be burned. The writer says the land that produces thorns and thistles is worthless, and its curse is imminent. Then he adds, “In the end it will be burned.” It's a sobering picture, friends.

The answer is salvation. The writer says he is convinced of “…better things in your case…” and he means things that accompany salvation. After the heavy part, friends, that's a deep breath of good news. He calls them beloved right before he says it.

The answer is work. The writer says, “For God is not unjust. He will not forget your work and the love you have shown for His name…” That's good news for anybody who's kept showing up, bakers. God sees every batch.

The answer is False. The writer says they have ministered to the saints “…and continue to do so.” Notice that second part, friends, because it means they're still going. That's a nice thing to hear after the thorns.

The answer is diligence. The writer says, “We want each of you to show this same diligence to the very end, in order to make your hope sure.” Diligence just means keeping at it, bakers. Like a timer that keeps ticking until the batch is done.

The answer is faith and patience. The writer says they will imitate those who “…through faith and patience inherit what has been promised.” Faith trusts, and patience waits. Waiting on a batch is easy compared to that, friends.
